stories.headline: India pledges help to rebuild school in flood-ravaged Nepal
stories.title: India pledges help to rebuild school in flood-ravaged Nepal
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: TRISHULI BAZAAR (NUWAKOT, NEPAL): India assured support for complete reconstruction of flood-ravaged Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Bidur, two days after TOI reported that the institution was seeking New Delhi's help to rebuild on higher, safer ground.

The assurance came less than a week after around 900 students on campus escaped the Aug 26 flash flood following an emergency evacuation, while hundreds more travelling to school were stopped from entering the danger zone.
Indian ambassador to Nepal Naveen Srivastava met the school's principal Rajendra Dawadi Tuesday.
Srivastava recalled the institution's long association with India, including construction of its newer building through Indian grant assistance.
He said Dawadi's timely action had saved lives of over 1,600 schoolchildren.
TOI had earlier reported how around 900 students were inside the school when warnings came, while buses carrying hundreds of others were stopped before reaching the danger zone.
Dawadi told TOI after the meeting with Srivastava on Wednesday: "We are deeply grateful to India for the reassurance and for standing with us at this difficult time.
The assurance has given the entire school community hope at a time when we are trying to restart classes and also looking for a safe location for a permanent campus.

Our entire school infrastructure has been destroyed, so our immediate priority is to bring the students back to classrooms." The flood has swept away virtually the entire campus, including its 18-room, three-storey academic block.
The school's two buses were among the few assets left.
Two staffers - non-teaching employee Chulrim Lama and secondary teacher Santos Parihar - still remain missing.

stories.headline: Public protest reflects failure to address grievances by NC Govt: LOP
stories.title: Public protest reflects failure to address grievances by NC Govt: LOP
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 2: Leader of Opposition (LOP) and senior Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Sunil Sharma on Wednesday launched a sharp attack on Chief Minister Omar Abdullah-led government, saying the large public participation in the BJP’s protest in Srinagar reflected growing discontent over what he termed the administration’s failure to address people’s concerns. “Thousands of people took to the streets against CM Omar-led government. This is a reflection of its failure, where people are worried and their problems remain unresolved,” Sharma said. He alleged that the government had failed the youth and “snatched away” their rights, particularly on issues concerning employment and recruitment. “That is why these people have come out on the streets,” he said. Sharma said the government’s alleged failures were now visible on the streets, claiming that the issues being raised by protesters were directly linked to the everyday concerns of the people. The BJP protest, led by J&K unit president and Rajya Sabha MP Sat Sharma and LOP Sunil Sharma, began at Ghanta Ghar in Lal Chowk, with party workers marching towards the civil secretariat. Protesters raised slogans against the government over unemployment, electricity tariffs, alleged corruption, recruitment issues, and other governance-related concerns. The BJP also highlighted the recent 6.83 percent electricity tariff hike, alleged backdoor appointments, and outsourcing of government jobs, besides the reported failure to implement the promise of 200 units of free electricity. Police and paramilitary personnel intercepted the march near Hari Singh High Street, short of the civil secretariat, amid heightened security arrangements in central Srinagar. Roads around Lal Chowk were also closed to vehicular movement as security forces were deployed at several strategic points. Addressing party workers, Sharma said the BJP protest was focused on four major issues — alleged irregularities in government recruitment, delay in holding local body and panchayat elections, corruption, and the increase in electricity tariffs. He accused the government of failing to adequately address issues related to electricity, water, roads, unemployment, and other basic concerns while continuing to focus its political narrative on restoration of statehood. Sharma also challenged CM Omar to resign from his Ganderbal Assembly seat and seek a fresh mandate from the people on the issue of statehood. “If you have any self-respect left, fight an election on it. Only then will we acknowledge it as your issue,” he said.

stories.headline: Maha Kumbh, SIR: Inside RaGa's Nashik visit
stories.title: Maha Kumbh, SIR: Inside RaGa's Nashik visit
stories.summary: Mumbai: Alleged corruption in the Nashik Kumbh mela and land acquisition for the ambitious ₹1 lakh crore Shakti Peeth expressway may become part of national political discourse, with Maharashtra Congress leaders apprising Rahul Gandhi about these issues on Wednesday. Gandhi was in Nashik to address leaders at the conclusion of Maharashtra Congress' 10-day organisational training camp."There has been a lot of corruption in the infrastructure works taken up during the Nashik Kumbh mela. We spoke to him about how there is no project report for the Kumbh mela and people were not taken into confidence. The entire project seems to be to get contracts for some chosen contractors and get 40% commission," senior Congress leader Prithviraj Chavan said after the meeting.Also Read: Nashik Kumbh Mela 2027: Maharashtra government approves Rs 2,267 crore to acquire 191.21 acres of landHe said that leaders also apprised him about farmer distress and farmers' opposition to land acquisition for the Shakti Peeth Expressway. They also updated him on the SIR exercise in the state which has deleted 2 crore voters from the list. Gandhi on Tuesday took to social media and asked: "Maharashtra 2024: Suddenly 3.9 million voters were added between the Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha elections. I said it then and I say it today. This was vote theft... And now in Maharashtra, 2.07 crore voters have been removed from the draft list - that's every fifth voter. Which list was correct," he asked."BJP and the 'Vote Theft Commission' keep changing their tactics and they will continue to do so - the goal remains just one: BJP's victory at any cost, and the end of India's democracy," he added.Congress in Maharashtra has got a second wind after the recent students' protests and Gandhi's visit to Pune last month, where he highlighted issues pertaining to tribal students in the state which forced the state government to negotiate with tribal students to accept their demands.Also Read: 'Holistic' preparations underway for Nashik Kumbh Mela but it's a race against time, say authoritiesBJP carried out protests in Nashik against Rahul Gandhi, claiming Congress was against women's reservation. BJP spokesman Navnath Ban asked why Gandhi had not taken action against a Congress leader in whose ashram school in Gadchiroli three girl students died of snake bite last month.

stories.headline: Can solar power finally break J&K’s electricity crisis cycle?
stories.title: Can solar power finally break J&K’s electricity crisis cycle?
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 2: Jammu and Kashmir’s recurring electricity crisis may have a partial solution in three developments already taking shape — rooftop solar, smart metering and the newly introduced Time-of-Day (ToD) tariff. Taken together, these measures could reduce dependence on costly grid power, flatten peak demand and, over time, help contain electricity costs. The government has already begun with its own buildings. A major rooftop solarisation programme covering thousands of government establishments is under implementation, with official plans running into hundreds of megawatts. The programme provides for net metering and bidirectional smart meters, allowing government buildings to consume their own solar generation and feed surplus electricity into the grid. JERC’s new ToD tariff can complement this effort. Consumers with sanctioned load above 10 kW and compatible metering are eligible for a 20 percent rebate during the 9 am-5 pm solar period, while specified peak-hour consumption attracts a surcharge. Government offices, colleges, universities and other institutions largely function during these daytime hours. They can therefore benefit from the rebate even before their rooftop systems are fully installed. Once solarised, their dependence on grid electricity during the day could fall further. This should now become an accountability issue for the Finance and Power Departments. Government establishments should identify every flexible load that can be shifted towards solar hours. Pumping stations, lift and irrigation schemes, workshops, and similar operations should be examined individually. Where storage or operational flexibility permits, there is little logic in running heavy loads during the evening peak when they could instead be operated during periods of abundant solar generation. The benefit would extend beyond government electricity bills. Every flexible load shifted away from the evening peak releases grid capacity precisely when households need electricity most for heating, cooking and lighting. Better demand management could therefore help reduce the pressure that contributes to winter curtailments. Industry should be the next major participant. The existing J&K Industrial Policy provides substantial support for DG sets. The policy is now under revision, and the government has emphasised green energy and reducing industry’s carbon footprint during stakeholder consultations. If the revised policy ultimately replaces or redirects conventional DG-set support towards rooftop solar, it would represent a logical transition — from subsidising diesel-based backup to supporting clean captive generation. The new framework should make such a transition meaningful enough to encourage existing industries to participate as well. The combination with ToD makes the case particularly relevant for Kashmir’s single-shift industries. A unit operating predominantly between 9 am and 5 pm can benefit from the existing daytime tariff rebate, while rooftop solar can meet a significant share of its electricity requirement during the same period. JAKEDA has also identified grid-connected rooftop solar across commercial and industrial sectors as a means of substantially reducing electricity drawn from the utility grid. But the biggest opportunity lies with households. The sheer number of domestic consumers means that even modest changes in household generation and consumption patterns could have a significant system-wide impact. J&K already has a substantial household rooftop-solar programme under way. Official information placed before Parliament showed 39,160 rooftop installations completed against 85,908 applications as of July 28, 2026. During the preceding five years, Rs 278.55 crore in central assistance had been released to J&K under rooftop-solar programmes. The gap between applications and completed installations, however, shows the scale of the unfinished task. Domestic solarisation now needs to be pursued with considerably greater urgency. There is another policy gap. Ordinary households are currently outside the JERC ToD provision because it applies to consumers above 10 kW. That leaves the largest consumer base without the very incentive that could encourage changes in consumption behaviour. As smart metering expands, the government could consider approaching JERC for a dedicated domestic ToD incentive for smart-metered consumers. Such a mechanism need not initially impose a peak-hour surcharge. A meaningful daytime rebate alone could encourage households to shift flexible consumption — washing, ironing, water heating, pumping and other electricity-intensive activities - towards solar hours. Nor should the policy necessarily wait until every household in J&K has a smart meter. The incentive could progressively be extended wherever compatible metering, billing and regulatory systems permit. The sequence is therefore straightforward. government can lead by solarising its buildings and shifting flexible loads into daylight hours. Industry and commerce can follow through rooftop solar and ToD incentives. Households can be brought into the solar programme at greater speed and gradually offered incentives to consume more electricity during the day. For decades, J&K’s electricity debate has focused primarily on one question: how much more power can the system generate or purchase? The next phase should ask two additional questions: how much electricity can be generated where it is consumed, and when should the remaining grid power be consumed? Solarise the roofs. Incentivise daytime consumption. Reduce the evening peak. If rooftop solar, smart metering and ToD tariffs are pursued as parts of one integrated demand-management strategy rather than as disconnected programmes, J&K may finally begin addressing not only its power deficit, but the structural pattern that keeps producing an electricity crisis.
